final.title: What contact decay hides in a small business
final.body:
Contact decay is not usually a grand strategy problem. In a 1–10 person business, it is the quiet point where a lead, customer, or supplier contact goes stale and nobody notices until the work is already harder to recover. That can live in a CRM, an inbox, or a spreadsheet with neat columns and weak follow-up. The real question is visibility: if you cannot see which contacts have gone quiet, you do not know whether you have a sales issue, a process issue, or just a memory issue. Human memory is a brave little filing system.

The practical next step is manual. Take one week of your contact list and mark every record you know has gone dormant. Then note how you found out: a missed reply, an old quote, a customer who never came back, or a stale note you found too late. That gives you a clean boundary for the decision. If the quiet contacts are already in digital tools and are easy to spot once you look, a lightweight flag in your existing workflow may be worth building. If most contacts arrive by phone or walk-in, AI may not fit.

You do not need to automate everything. First see where contact decay is hiding, and whether it is real work you are still doing by hand.
